The Wonga pigeon (Leucosarcia melanoleuca) is a large, ground-dwelling columbid endemic to the moist forests of eastern Australia, and its life history traits reflect a slow-paced reproductive strategy characteristic of many rainforest birds. Field observations indicate that hatchlings emerge after an incubation period of 17 days [ab = 17 days] maintained at an average nest temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a duration that is relatively brief compared to other pigeon species of similar body size. The hatchling itself emerges at a modest initial wet weight of 16.5 grams [Ww0 = 16.5 grams], a value that underscores the altricial state of the neonate and the substantial parental investment required during the subsequent nestling phase. This low birth mass is consistent with a strategy of producing relatively small clutches, as the species lays exactly 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch] and typically completes only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], yielding an annual reproductive output of 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year] that is markedly constrained in comparison to many temperate columbids.

The developmental trajectory of the nestling proceeds through distinct milestones under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active metabolic period, which corresponds to a body temperature of approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Within this thermal regime, fledging occurs at 26.5 days after hatching [tx = 26.5 days after hatching], a comparatively rapid transition to flight that may reflect predation pressure on ground nests at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Following fledging, the juvenile enters a prolonged sub-adult phase, with puberty — defined by the onset of gonadal maturation — reached at 80 days after hatching [tp = 80 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively late attainment of sexual maturity relative to the fledging date suggests that a substantial period of somatic growth and feather development is necessary before reproductive competence is achieved, a pattern commonly observed in species that invest heavily in a small number of offspring.

Sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size is evident in the adult population, with the asymptotic mass differing noticeably between the sexes. Females attain a maximum adult body mass of 448.15 grams [Wwi = 448.15 grams], while males reach a somewhat lower ultimate wet weight of 410 grams [Wwi = 410 grams]. This size discrepancy, in which females are on average approximately nine percent heavier than males, is typical of many columbids and may be linked to the metabolic demands of egg production and incubation. Under the thermal conditions that define their active metabolic state at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the maximum achieved lifespan of the species has been recorded at 14 years [am = 14 years], a longevity that is substantial for a bird of this body mass and aligns with the slow life-history pace expected for a tropical or subtropical rainforest specialist that faces relatively low extrinsic mortality.

Basal metabolic rate measurements provide insight into the energetic costs of maintaining this slow life-history strategy. Respirometry trials conducted under standard conditions at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] indicate that the species has a resting oxygen consumption of 301 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 301 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate, when considered alongside the relatively long lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years], suggests a moderate pace of life that is intermediate between the high-metabolism, short-lived species of open habitats and the extremely low-metabolism, long-lived species of stable environments at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. The first successful reproductive event, marking the initiation of breeding activity, occurs at 2.3 years after hatching [tR = 2.3 years after hatching], a delay that presumably allows the bird to reach full skeletal maturity and to secure a suitable territory within the dense forest understory at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C].

These combined life-history parameters paint a portrait of a species that has evolved a conservative reproductive strategy in response to the ecological constraints of its environment. The adult female body mass of 448.15 grams [Wwi = 448.15 grams] and the adult male mass of 410 grams [Wwi = 410 grams] highlight a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism, while the hatchling weight of 16.5 grams [Ww0 = 16.5 grams] is typical for a precocial-altricial intermediate. The incubation period of 17 days [ab = 17 days] at 39 °C [T = 39 °C] and the fledging period of 26.5 days after hatching [tx = 26.5 days after hatching] at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] indicate a compressed early development, yet the onset of puberty is deferred to 80 days after hatching [tp = 80 days after hatching] and first breeding to 2.3 years after hatching [tR = 2.3 years after hatching], representing a clear life-history delay. With a maximum lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years], the Wonga pigeon exemplifies a slow-reproducing, long-lived bird that invests heavily in each of its two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and single annual clutch [F_R_i = single annual clutch], yielding a modest annual reproductive output of 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year] — a trade-off that reflects the species' adaptation to the stable, resource-limited conditions of its rainforest habitat at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C].
